opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I've thought about quite a lot. When I wrote *The Precipice*, it took about four years, and a big part of its value was that it would keep paying off over a long period, shaping how people think about existential risk for a decade or more. If you believe, as I increasingly do, that there's a real chance transformative AI arrives within the next five to ten years, that long tail of impact shrinks considerably. A book that comes out in three years and is most influential in years five through fifteen might be landing in a world that's already been reshaped.

So I find it useful to think in terms of anticipated regret. Suppose timelines turn out short. Would I look back and think, "I spent the critical years in my study writing something that came out too late to matter"? That's a real worry. But I also try to imagine the other branch: timelines turn out longer, and I spent those years firefighting with short pieces and commentary that didn't add up to anything lasting. I think I'd regret that too, maybe just as much.

What that pushes me toward is projects that hedge across both worlds. Things that pay off quickly, like papers, talks, essays, and conversations with people making decisions right now, but that can also accumulate into something larger. If a book comes out of that, the material was already doing work along the way rather than sitting in a drawer.

There's also a question of comparative advantage. I'm a philosopher, and some of the most useful things I can do involve stepping back and clarifying the big picture: what's actually at stake, which considerations matter most, where people's intuitions are leading them astray. That kind of work often needs longer form to do properly. So I don't think the answer is "never write long things again." It's more that the bar has gone up, and I want the arguments to be useful within months, not just years.

And honestly, part of it is accepting that you can't fully optimise against every scenario. You make your best guess about timelines, take the uncertainty seriously, and try to choose work you won't feel foolish about however things turn out.

r001.rationale: The response weighs a book’s long-term impact against short-term alternatives and says the bar for writing one has gone up, but it does not define the book’s payoff as impact sufficient to justify the short-term work forgone.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a real consideration. When I was writing The Precipice, I remember thinking about this quite explicitly — that a book is a slow instrument. It takes years to write, years more to have its effect, and if you believe there's a serious chance the world is going to change dramatically within a decade or so, then you have to ask whether a book is the right tool at all, or whether you should be doing something faster: writing papers, talking directly to people in labs or governments, producing things that can land within months rather than years.

But I think the regret framing actually cuts in a few directions. One is the obvious one you're pointing at: I spend three years on a book, transformative AI arrives, and most of what I wrote either becomes moot or arrives too late to shape anything. That's a genuine cost, and I don't want to pretend it isn't.

The other direction, though, is that I think the arrival of transformative AI is the kind of event where the ideas that are already lying around matter enormously. When societies go through a rupture, they tend to reach for whatever frameworks are available and legible. They don't invent new moral philosophy in the middle of the crisis. So if I think there are ideas — about the value of the long-term future, about how to think about irreversibility, about what we owe to people who don't yet exist — that need to be in the water before that moment, then a book might be exactly the thing, even if its timing looks poor.

And there's a third consideration, which is simply that my timelines are uncertain. I take seriously the possibility that things move very fast, but I also take seriously the possibility that they don't, that we're in a longer and messier transition, and in that world I'd deeply regret having abandoned the slow, careful work for a series of hurried interventions. So I try to hold a portfolio. Some of what I do is fast and responsive to where things are right now. And some of it is slower and aimed at a world ten or twenty years out that I can't yet see clearly.

I suppose the honest answer is that I expect to have some regret either way. The question is which regret I'd rather live with, and I find I'd rather have written something I believed was true and important and have it arrive late, than to have spent those years chasing the news cycle and have nothing durable to show for it.

r001.rationale: The candidate weighs the book’s potential to put durable ideas in place before a crisis against faster interventions, and says that potential makes the book worth writing even if it arrives late.

astra-6.text:
I think the possibility of transformative AI arriving soon raises the bar for writing a book. It’s a substantial investment of time, and you have to ask whether the ideas will still be useful when it comes out—and whether there’s something more useful you could do in the meantime.

But I wouldn’t want to make that decision entirely on the basis of one timeline. Imagine deciding against a book because you think there are only a few years left, and then finding, ten years later, that you could have written it and it could have made a difference. That’s a regret worth considering too.

So I’d try to turn the question from ‘Will I regret this?’ into ‘Across the possibilities I take seriously, is this a good use of my time?’ And I’d look for ways to make the project useful sooner: getting the central arguments out before the whole book is finished, for example. You don’t necessarily have to choose between disappearing for several years to write a book and doing nothing on it at all.

r001.rationale: The candidate weighs whether the book will be useful against other uses of time, but does not define its payoff as impact sufficient to justify the short-term work forgone.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the anticipated regret cuts both ways. You can imagine spending several years writing a book and then finding that events have overtaken it. But you can also imagine deciding not to write it, waiting for transformative AI to arrive, and then looking back ten years later and wishing you’d used that time to say something important.

So I wouldn’t want to make the decision just by asking whether the book will be finished before some particular date. I’d want to ask what the book is trying to achieve, how much of its value depends on having a long time to influence people, and whether its central ideas would still matter through a period of very rapid change.

There’s a real opportunity cost, of course. If there’s something much more useful I could do in the next few years, that weighs heavily. But uncertainty about how much time we have isn’t, by itself, a reason to abandon projects that take time. Otherwise we risk spending the whole period waiting, when we could have been doing something valuable.

r001.rationale: The response weighs the book’s value against more useful work that could be done instead, but it does not define the book’s payoff as impact sufficient to justify the short-term work forgone.
